messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am trying to speed up my computations with the parallel option, but it 
seems to be slower than using only one CPU core. I don't know a lot 
about the snow package or the parallel argument. Perhaps you can give me 
a hint how I can achieve faster estimation runs. Here is a 
self-contained example of what I have tried on a multicore CPU running 
Linux:

#snow and rlecuyer are installed
library(network)
library(ergm)
set.seed(1234)

test <- function(x, p=0) {
   mat <- matrix(rbinom(400,1,0.09), nrow=20)
   nw <- network(mat)
   ergm(nw ~ edges + twopath, control=control.ergm(seed=1234,
     parallel=p))
}

single <- system.time(lapply(1:20, test, p=0))
multiple <- system.time(lapply(1:20, test, p=2))

print(single)

#   user  system elapsed
# 94.873   0.012  95.073

print(multiple)

#   user  system elapsed
# 48.560   2.040 521.141

So apparently using two cores is much slower than using only one core. I 
checked my system monitor and indeed two cores are fully used during the 
second run above. What do I have to do in order to get it running 
properly? I didn't find any documentation of this, but perhaps I didn't 
look in the right places?

Many thanks

Philip

messages.subject: [statnet_help] including nodeicov, nodeocov, and edgecov in same model
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] including nodeicov, nodeocov, and edgecov in same model
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have a question that seems pretty simple, but I haven't been able to find out a clear answer about it yet.


I have directed network data with a valued trait (X), and my theory stipulates the following:

1.? actors high in X will send fewer ties to others (actor-level hypothesis -- nodeocov)

2.? actors high in X trait will receive more ties from others (actor-level hypothesis -- nodeicov)

?

3. actors will tend to send ties to those who are higher in X than themselves (dyadic-level hypothesis).


Is it legitimate to specify an ERGM equation that simultaneously includes nodeicov, nodeocov, and a term that accounts for dyadic differences in X?? It seems that a dyadic difference term is completely determined by the information contained in the nodeocov and the nodeicov terms, but I am wanting to understand both nodal and dyadic factors.? 


Also, I'm using "edgecov" to denote raw difference in X between nodes (using a matrix of difference scores), rather than the absolute difference term (absdiff), because point #3 above indicates raw difference as the important issue. Is it appropriate to include this edgecov term alongside the other two terms (nodeocov and nodeicov), or is there too much redundant information in the model?



thanks,
markus schafer
dept of sociology

University of Toronto

messages.subject: [statnet_help] including nodeicov, nodeocov, and edgecov in same model
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] including nodeicov, nodeocov, and edgecov in same model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Markus,

What you propose as a model is possible, depending on the parameterization 
you use.  The design is a bit like a mixing matrix with dyads cross 
tabulated by attribute X.  Your model has row and column effects, and an 
"upper triangle" effect.

What you need to be clear about is whether the magnitude of (X_i - X_j) 
matters.  If not, you can construct a binary indicator for the edgecov, 
and the terms will not be collinear.  If the magnitude matters, but only 
when the difference is < 0, the edgecov will =0 for cases when the diff is 
>0, so will still not be collinear.  You may still run into some 
difficulties estimating this, depending on the size of your 
sample and distribution of your data.

What you can't do is put the difference in, along with the values of X_i 
and X_j, but it sounds like your theory would not lead to that 
operationalization anyway.

hth,
Martina

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Edge attributes / Multiple Networks / Signed Networks
messages.body_plain:
Hello!

Our data is about sociolinguistic relations of several teenage students 
(12 years old) in sociocentric networks of multiple schools. The 
sociolinguistic relations have two types of information: relations 
between adolescents and language used in this relation. Not all dyads 
have relations, and if relations exist, can be in language A or language 
B. Our information can be more complex, because language use is in 
language A, language B, language A and B, o other languages. But we can 
dichotomize the data.

We have problems with the analysis of our data, because edges have 
attributes, and and I couldn't find any reference about how to handle 
whit it, neither with R nor any other software.

Then, I have three questions:

How can we analyse edge attributes with ERGM? Is it possible? A possible 
way is work with multiple networks, like "relations in language A" and 
"relations in language B". As I see in (few) previous posts in this 
direction in this mail list, high statistical knowledge is needed to 
proceed. Out of R, it is possible compare networks with ERG Models with 
XPnet. But our data is (theorically) negative correspondence, and can't 
interpret results of multiple networks analysis like it. Do you know 
bibliography that can help us?

How can we analyse valued networks (qualitative links) with "sna"? We 
are interested in multiple analysis at the descriptive level:: language 
reciprocity, centrality in different languages, triad analysis with 
multiple languages relations, and so on...  We are working it combining 
UCINET results of full network, and network in language A and network in 
language B, and comparing it with Excel. Is it possible analyse wit 
"sna" how reciprocity dyads have language reciprocity too? For exemple, 
"90% of reciprocity relations are in the same language". Or 20% of 
transitive triads use A language in X -> Y and Y -> Z relations, and B 
language in X -> Z relation. We are also interested in some analysis 
with "sna" like UCINET> Tools> Testing Hypotheses> Mixed Dyadic / Nodal> 
Categorical attributes> Relational Contingency Table analysis.

Maybe a solution is working with signed networks. Origins of this 
analysis is other, about positive relations (friends) and negative 
relations (enemies). And balanced networks theory don't adjust to 
language networks. But is not far that language use in networks can be 
understanded  like relations in A language (+), in B language (-) or in 
both languages (0). How can we work with signed networks in "statnet"?

Last but not least, my presentation in Statnet mailing list: I am Natxo 
Sorolla, and I am working in sociology of language at the University of 
Barcelona.

Natxo Sorolla

remaining observations (risking some bias if more than just a few

Philip
